Step 01 · Prepare · 5 Nov

Plan the gates done

Question. Decide what to test, in what order, and what each test must show before money or time goes into the next step.

Result. Gated plan: the cheapest question that can kill the plan goes first.

What we did

  • Wrote the gated rollout plan (gates 0.1, G0-G5) and researched the censorship facts.
  • Chose VLESS + Reality as the main protocol, AmneziaWG 3.1 for phones, a commercial service as backup (D-02).
  • Chose GL-MT3000 routers, two identical units (D-06).

Next time

  • Write the privacy rules (what may be published) on day one, next to the plan.

Step 02 · Probe Russia · 5 Nov

Phase 0: Russian PC done

Question. Is the remote Russian PC usable as a probe and representative of Russian internet?

Result. PASS: tools run without admin, regular ISP, filtering visible.

What we did

  • Quick check package over Remote Desktop: PowerShell, curl, no proxy, no HTTPS inspection.
  • Blocked sites time out, LinkedIn fails TLS: the filter is visible from this line.

Problems met and how we got past them

L13 Remote-desktop sessions to the Russian PC are short.

Fix: One package for several phases; links re-read every cycle; evidence rewritten every cycle.

Rule: Design packages around the session window, not around the phase list.

Next time

  • Plan every package around the short Remote Desktop window (one package, several phases).

Step 06 · Server A · 6 Nov

Key-only SSH done

Question. No password login on the server, proven, not assumed.

Result. Password login off, verified from outside.

What we did

  • The hoster's image kept password login on despite our setting; fixed and verified with sshd -T and a clean outside test.

Problems met and how we got past them

L1 Time4VPS Ubuntu image: the main sshd_config says PasswordAuthentication yes before our drop-in; sshd takes the first value, so password login stayed on.

Fix: setup-server.sh neutralises conflicting lines in the main file and checks sshd -T.

Rule: Verify the effective state, never only the written config (D-09).

L2 A "password disabled" test from the Mac still logged in with the key (agent/config).

Fix: ssh -F /dev/null -o IdentityAgent=none -o PubkeyAuthentication=no -o PreferredAuthentications=password

Rule: Negative tests must remove every other path to success.

Files: server/ssh-hardening-fix.sh, server/EXECUTION-RECORD.md

Back to the path

Step 07 · Server A · 8 Nov

Server A setup done

Question. Hardened server with the VPN entry points, configured by one repeatable script.

Result. Xray running: Vision on 443, XHTTP on 8443; firewall, fail2ban, auto-updates.

What we did

  • setup-server.sh v1.1 failed on the real server (Xray could not read its config); v1.2 fixed it the same day.
  • Camouflage site auto-picked from the server's own network; links saved to the password manager.

Problems met and how we got past them

L3 Xray's official installer now runs the service as user xray; v1.1 gave the config to nogroup -> "permission denied", Xray down.

Fix: v1.2 reads the service user from systemd, sets root:<group> 640, then checks the user can read it.

Rule: Do not assume a third-party installer's defaults; check them at run time.

L4 Sourcing /etc/os-release overwrote the script's VERSION; evidence said "v24.04.5".

Fix: Renamed to SCRIPT_VERSION (v1.3).

Rule: Never name script variables after common environment/OS variables.

L14 Traffic to the VPS went through the corporate GlobalProtect tunnel; the server saw the employer's address.

Fix: Disconnect GP from its menu before server work.

Rule: Check the route (route -n get <ip>) before any server step.

L15 The work Mac is employer-managed (MDM); stopping the GP agent cut all network access (enforcement).

Fix: Never disable the extension or enforcement (D-16). Longer term: manage servers from an own device.

Rule: Do not defeat an employer control.

L17 The agent's guard forbids remote shells and (in the old workspace) writes outside it.

Fix: The user runs server commands; files are staged and copied with one rsync. This repo is inside the agent's workspace, so writes work here.

Rule: Plan for the user executing; give one command per step and say where it runs.

L18 A pasted command block once included its trailing stop command; a domain inside a command became a link.

Fix: Minimal blocks; no bare domains in commands.

Rule: Give only what runs now.

Next time

  • Test setup-server.sh end to end in a container with the real Xray installer before the first real run.

Files: evidence/EVIDENCE-phase2b-server-20261107-215823.txt, server/setup-server.sh

Step 08 · Prove from Russia · 8 Nov

Phase 2b: tunnel test done

Question. Does the VPN itself get through the filter: exit address, repeated requests, big download, blocked sites?

Result. PASS: 4 of 5 variants; all three Vision fingerprints; ~20 Mbit/s.

What we did

  • Five variants (Vision x3 fingerprints, XHTTP x2) through a local proxy on the Russian PC; Xray bundled in the zip.
  • Blocked sites reached; sites refusing Russian users opened; two HTTP 400 answers were script artefacts.

Problems met and how we got past them

L9 facebook.com and web.whatsapp.com answer HTTP 400 to scripts through a working tunnel; counted as "blocked".

Fix: Any HTTP answer = reached; censorship shows as timeout/reset (monitor v1.1).

Rule: Classify by transport outcome, not by HTTP status.

L10 sberbank.ru failed on every variant (curl exit 60).

Fix: Not a tunnel issue: Russian national CA not trusted by default.

Rule: Know your control sites; exclude ones with their own failure modes.

L16 GitHub downloads failed (HTTP 503/504) while GP was connected.

Fix: Disconnect GP, or download elsewhere and pass XRAY_ZIP=; the checksum is verified either way.

Rule: Bundle binaries in packages; pin version and SHA-256.

Next time

  • Count any HTTP answer as 'reached' from the start (L9).

Files: evidence/EVIDENCE-phase2b-tunnel-20261108-195210.txt, windows/phase2b2c-EXECUTED/

Back to the path

Step 09 · Prove from Russia · 8-9 Nov

Phase 2c: 12 h monitor done

Question. Does it keep working over hours, including the evening peak, not just for 15 minutes?

Result. PASS: 289/289 cycles on both links, evening covered, no gaps.

What we did

  • Restartable monitor: one line every 2.5 min, evidence rewritten every cycle, single instance via a lock.
  • Two bugs found in Docker before first use; the Windows-only parts (keep-awake, stop, restart) proven on the real PC.

Problems met and how we got past them

L8 PowerShell variable names ignore case: loop variable $e overwrote the evidence list $E; a silent catch {} hid it, so no evidence file was written (monitor v1.0).

Fix: Renamed; save errors are shown on screen (v1.1). A scan for case-colliding variable names is part of the test.

Rule: Never swallow errors in the path that writes evidence.

L11 1 MB per-cycle checks read 7-11 Mbit/s while the 20 MB test showed ~20 Mbit/s.

Fix: Use the 20 MB figure for capacity.

Rule: Monitor v1.2: add a periodic large download (NEXT-STEPS 2).

L12 The first monitor start was closed after one cycle.

Fix: Restart-by-design worked: new file, stale lock taken over, leftover xray cleaned.

Rule: Long runs must be restartable by a non-expert without thinking.

L19 Docker Desktop could not see the agent's /private/tmp scratch folder (empty mounts).

Fix: docker create + docker cp instead of -v.

L20 mcr.microsoft.com/powershell:latest pulled a non-arm64 image on Apple silicon (exec format error).

Fix: ubuntu:22.04 + the official PowerShell linux-arm64 tarball + libicu70.

L21 A killed process stayed a zombie and looked "alive" to the lock check.

Fix: Run test containers with --init (Windows has no zombies; test artefact).

L22 pkill -f "client-1.json" killed the test's own shell (its command line contained the pattern).

Fix: Read the PID from the lock file and kill it; never pkill -f with a pattern the caller's command line contains.

Next time

  • Add a periodic large download and fingerprint rotation to the monitor (step 13).

Files: evidence/EVIDENCE-phase2c-monitor-20261108-200950.txt, windows/phase2b2c-EXECUTED/phase2c-monitor.ps1

Step 10 · Operate · 9 Nov

Key rotation done

Question. Links had been on a machine we do not control: make them worthless.

Result. All secrets replaced; old links refused; camouflage kept.

What we did

  • rotate-keys.sh: new client ID, Reality keys, short ID, XHTTP path; validated before switching; tested in Docker first.

Problems met and how we got past them

L5 Xray refused a temp config named config.json.new-...: it picks the format from the extension.

Fix: Temp file config.new-<stamp>.json.

Rule: Keep the real extension on temp files.

L6 The camouflage auto-pick chose a different neighbour on the second setup run.

Fix: Key rotation (rotate-keys.sh) keeps the camouflage; never FORCE=1 setup just to change keys.

Rule: Change one variable at a time once something passed.

L7 Links were placed on a machine we do not control -> treated as leaked.

Fix: rotate-keys.sh replaced UUID, Reality keys, short ID, XHTTP path; old links refused.

Rule: Testers get their own client ID (manage-clients.sh, D-19).

Next time

  • Give every tester their own client ID so nothing needs rotating (step 14).

Files: evidence/EVIDENCE-rotate-keys-20261109-055215.txt, server/rotate-keys.sh

If we started fresh: do these from day one

  6. Keep the repo publish-safe from the first commit: private values in .private/, the pre-commit guard on.

Reliable internet from Russia · explainer · updated 2026-11-08 after Phase 2b

How the VPN chain works, and why we check so much

Your traffic has to cross a Russian filter that judges four things: where it goes, what protocol it looks like, which site name it mentions, and how it behaves over time. Each check in the plan tests one point in the chain where the filter can cut it. The server side is built and verified, and on 8 November the tunnel passed its first test from Russia: 4 of 5 variants, all three Vision fingerprints, 6 of 6 repeated requests, a complete 20 MB download at up to 20.5 Mbit/s on a ~28 Mbit/s office line. Still untested: home ISPs, long runs and the work VPNs.

4 / 8
gates passed (Russian PC usable, hosters reachable, server A's address reachable, Phase 2b tunnel test for A)
1 / 2
servers running (A in Lithuania; B is bought next, after the monitor: decision D-17)
21
days to arrival in Russia (about 2026-11-29)

Written for the user: not a network specialist, wants the real mechanism. Technical terms are explained where they first appear and again in the glossary.

1. The chain: every hop your traffic makes

A web page or a work VPN connection from Russia passes six points. A failure at any one of them breaks everything after it, which is why the plan tests each point separately instead of only asking "does the VPN work?".

2. How the Russian filter decides what to cut

Every Russian ISP must install a TSPU box from the regulator (Roskomnadzor) in its network. It reads the traffic as it passes (deep packet inspection, DPI) and can drop, slow or reset connections. It does not need to break the encryption: the outside of a connection already tells it a lot. It applies roughly five tests. Each card says what it looks at and how our setup answers it.

TEST 1

Where is it going?

Lists of blocked addresses. Since August 2026 whole address blocks (subnets) of hosters popular for VPNs are blocked. From the Russian PC, Hetzner, OVH and Linode were completely blocked.

Answer: hosters that tested clean from Russia (Time4VPS, BuyVM) and a second server at a different hoster as a spare.

TEST 2

What protocol is it?

Classic VPNs have recognisable handshakes. Plain WireGuard and OpenVPN have been blocked since February 2026 by exactly this test.

Answer: VLESS over TLS 1.3, byte for byte the same shape as a browser opening an HTTPS site.

TEST 3

Which site does it name?

The first message of an HTTPS connection carries the site name in plain text (the SNI field). Names of blocked sites are cut immediately.

Answer: the tunnel names an ordinary, unblocked site (the camouflage site), not the real destination.

TEST 4

How does it behave?

The filter lets a suspicious connection start, watches it, and silently stalls it after about 16 KB. From the Russian PC a Vultr Frankfurt download froze at exactly 15,957 bytes.

Answer: Vision flow-control hides the typical "tunnel inside TLS" rhythm; we test big downloads and long runs, not just one page.

TEST 5

What is the server really?

A censor can connect to a suspicious address itself and see whether a real website answers (active probing). This is documented for China's filter; general knowledge, not confirmed for Russia.

Answer: Reality: anyone without our key is passed through to a real website and sees its real certificate.

BEYOND REACH

Whitelist mode

In many regions mobile internet is sometimes switched to "only allowlisted addresses". Then no tunnel to a foreign server can work.

Answer: none technical: use home or hotel Wi-Fi via the router; friends' tests record when it happens.

3. How VLESS + Reality hides the tunnel

Xray is the program on the server and on your devices. VLESS is its lightweight tunnel protocol. Reality is the disguise: it makes the server look, to everyone except you, like an ordinary website that belongs to someone else.

The three extra knobs we test

  • Browser fingerprint (chrome, firefox, safari). Every browser builds its opening TLS message slightly differently. Xray copies one of them exactly (uTLS). Filters have been known to target one specific fingerprint, so we test three and keep the one that survives.
  • Vision (port 443) vs XHTTP (port 8443). Vision hides the give-away pattern of "an encrypted connection inside an encrypted connection" by passing the inner encryption straight through. XHTTP instead chops traffic into ordinary-looking HTTP requests. They fail in different ways, so having both doubles the chance one passes. The router's failover (URLTest) accepts only Vision, which is why Vision matters most.
  • Camouflage site. The name in the opening message. Today it is a neighbour's site; the next section explains why we want our own.

4. Why we want our own domain for the camouflage

Reality has to name some real site. Today our server names a neighbour's site: a small website on another server in the same hoster network. That works: Phase 2b passed with it from the Russian PC on 8 November. Our own domain ("self-steal") fixes three weaknesses of borrowing a stranger's site.

1. Consistency

A filter can look up the site name in public DNS and compare it with the address actually contacted. With a neighbour's site they disagree. With our domain they agree. We do not know that the Russian filter runs this check today; it is cheap for it to add.

2. Independence

Reality copies the camouflage site's live TLS behaviour. If the neighbour switches off TLS 1.3, changes certificate, moves, or goes offline, our connections start failing or start looking wrong. Our own site changes only when we change it.

3. Plausible traffic

A tunnel moves gigabytes. Gigabytes a day to a stranger's hobby site stand out; to "your own site on your own server" they look like a personal cloud or backup.

Cost and trade-offs. About $10 a year at an international registrar, a non-.ru name, with WHOIS privacy. The name itself can be blocked; then we buy another, which is cheap and fast. It also adds a small web server with an auto-renewing certificate to maintain.

Why not now. The neighbour's site passed Phase 2b from Russia, so the own domain is an upgrade for longevity, not urgent. We add it later and re-run the same test; if the tunnel ever starts failing, it is one of the first fixes to try.

5. Why the work laptop probably needs the router

Your work laptop runs two corporate VPNs. Neither is built to hide from a censor:

  • AWS Client VPN is built on OpenVPN, and plain OpenVPN has been blocked in Russia since February 2026. Directly from a Russian network it will very likely be cut by test 2.
  • GlobalProtect normally uses IPsec over UDP port 4501, with an HTTPS fallback. Its portal answered from the Russian PC, but its actual tunnel is untested.

Wrapped inside our outer tunnel, the filter never sees either of them: it sees only the outer VLESS + Reality connection. Doing that wrapping on the laptop would mean installing our VPN software on a company-managed machine. The router does it outside the laptop: the laptop just joins the WORK Wi-Fi network and runs its corporate VPNs as usual. That is gate G4, and the planned OpenVPN probe decides it.

One technical cost: a tunnel inside a tunnel leaves less room per packet (MTU). The router script clamps packet sizes (MSS clamping) so the inner VPN does not stall on large transfers.

6. Why we check so many details

Censorship failures are often partial: the first page loads, then a big file freezes; it works at noon and dies in the evening; it works on the office line and not at home. A single "it connected" proves very little. Each detail below catches one specific failure that a simpler test would miss.

8. What unblocks what

The plan is gated: the cheapest question that can kill the plan goes first, and money and time go into the next step only after the current one passes. Phase 2b on the Russian PC was the bottleneck; it passed on 8 November. The monitor (at least 3 hours including the evening, decision D-18) runs next; server B follows it (decision D-17).

Can be prepared now, without the Russian PC

  • The Russian-PC package phase2b2c (built and delivered; tunnel test run and passed; monitor running next). The router twin test is still to build.
  • The own-domain setup script, ready for when the domain is bought.
  • Client management for friends' keys and the friends' instructions (G3).
  • The temporary OpenVPN probe (G4) and the router kit (G5).

9. Every step as if-else

The plan is a chain of yes/no questions. Each diamond is a test; the answer decides the next step. A "no" never ends the project: it either sends us back to try the next fix (dashed "try again" arrows) or switches to a fallback. The four flows below run after the steps already done.

Done so far (5 to 8 November)

Nine steps, all passed, the last being the first tunnel test from Russia. One failed first and was fixed the same day: setup v1.1 could not start Xray because the Xray installer now runs it as a new user; v1.2 fixed it.

Glossary

TSPU
The filtering box Russian ISPs must install; it inspects passing traffic (DPI) and drops, slows or resets connections.
DPI
Deep packet inspection: judging traffic by its contents and patterns, not just its address.
TLS 1.3
The encryption under every HTTPS site. Its first message (the "hello") is partly readable.
SNI
The site name written in plain text inside the TLS hello. Filters read it.
Xray
The program on the server and on clients that runs the tunnel.
VLESS
Xray's tunnel protocol: a thin layer that carries your traffic inside TLS.
Reality
Xray's disguise: the server borrows a real site's TLS identity; only key holders get the tunnel, everyone else is passed to the real site.
Vision / XHTTP
Two ways of shaping tunnel traffic. Vision runs on port 443 and is what the router uses; XHTTP on 8443 is the backup variant.
Fingerprint (uTLS)
The exact byte pattern of a browser's TLS hello. Xray imitates Chrome, Firefox or Safari.
Self-steal
Reality pointing at our own domain and our own small website instead of a stranger's site.
Active probing
A censor connecting to a suspicious server to see what answers.
sing-box
Another tunnel program; Podkop on the router uses it. The "twin test" runs it on the Russian PC with the router's settings.
Podkop / OpenWrt
OpenWrt is open router firmware; Podkop is an add-on that sends chosen traffic through VLESS and fails over between servers (URLTest).
SOCKS proxy mode
How we test on the Russian PC: the tunnel serves only programs that ask for it, so Remote Desktop keeps working.
MTU / MSS clamping
Maximum packet size. Tunnels in tunnels shrink it; clamping prevents stalls.
AmneziaWG 3.1
A disguised WireGuard variant for phones; older versions (1.5, 2.0) are now detectable.

Reliable internet from Russia · router kit · 2026-11-08

Router arrival check: GL.iNet GL-MT3000 (Beryl AX)

Check every unit in two stages: five minutes at the pickup counter with the box still closed, then about thirty minutes at home on the factory firmware. Keep the units that pass every step; return the rest within the return window. Flash OpenWrt only after a unit has passed, and only on the main unit first.

5 min
at the counter, before you accept the parcel
30 min
at home per unit, factory firmware, no internet needed
2 kept
main + spare; any extra unit goes back within the return window

What to bring

  • Your phone, charged (photos, marketplace app with the pickup code).
  • This page, printed or on the phone; a pen for the record sheet.
  • At home: a USB-C charger of 5 V / 3 A (15 W) or more and a USB-C cable, a laptop or phone with Wi-Fi. An Ethernet cable is optional.

The flow

A. At the counter (box still closed)

Photograph the parcel and the box from all sides before opening anything. Marketplaces generally let you inspect appearance and contents at the pickup point and refuse there (rules differ per marketplace; check the order page).

Counter checks, in order
✓#CheckGenuine looks likeIf not
A1Model on the boxExactly GL-MT3000, "Beryl AX". Not MT2500, MT3600BE, MT6000.refuse
A2Seal and packagingFactory seal intact, box not crushed, not re-taped.refuse
A3Open the box, look at the unitNew: no scratches, protective film, no dust in the ports.refuse
A4Label on the bottomModel GL-MT3000, serial number, MAC address, Wi-Fi name like GL-MT3000-xxx and its password. Sticker not peeled or reprinted.refuse
A5ContentsRouter, USB-C power cable, Ethernet cable, quick-start leaflet. A power adapter may or may not be included, depending on region.photo, decide at home
A6Ports, by eyeTwo Ethernet ports (one marked WAN, 2.5G), one USB-A, one USB-C (power), a reset hole, a small side switch.refuse
A7Photograph the labelReadable photo of serial, MAC and Wi-Fi password. You will need it in step B.–
A8Version: Global or CNBox and quick-start leaflet in English or multilingual = Global (also sold as "international"). Chinese-only box and leaflet = CN (mainland China) version.CN: accept, spare only; B7 confirms

B. At home, factory firmware (per unit)

No internet needed. Do not plug anything into the WAN port yet. Check one unit at a time so labels and results do not get mixed up.

  1. B1. Power. Plug the USB-C cable into a 5 V / 3 A charger. The LED lights, then settles after 1–2 minutes. A weak phone charger causes reboots that look like a fault.
  2. B2. Wi-Fi from the label. On the laptop or phone, find the network named on the label (GL-MT3000-xxx and GL-MT3000-xxx-5G). Connect with the password from the label. Both 2.4 and 5 GHz should appear.
  3. B3. Admin page. Open http://192.168.8.1 in a browser. A GL.iNet setup page appears: choose a language and set an admin password (write it on the record sheet). Skip or decline any cloud account (GoodCloud).
  4. B4. Model and MAC. On the overview or system page, read the model and the MAC address. Model must be GL-MT3000; the MAC must match the label. Different interfaces may differ from the label only in the last one or two characters; that is normal.
  5. B5. Hardware check (strongest test). From a Mac or Linux terminal while connected to the router's Wi-Fi (Windows: PowerShell has ssh too). The password is the admin password from B3. 
    ssh root@192.168.8.1
    Then, on the router: 
    ubus call system board
free -m
cat /proc/device-tree/compatible; echo
cat /proc/gl-hw-info/country_code; echo
    Expected: "model": "GL.iNet GL-MT3000" and "board_name": "glinet,gl-mt3000"; free -m total about 490–500 MB (512 MB RAM minus reserved); the compatible line names glinet,gl-mt3000 and mediatek,mt7981; the country code is not CN (if it is, or the file is missing, note it for B7). Type exit to leave.
  6. B6. Wired port. Plug the laptop into the LAN port with the Ethernet cable (Wi-Fi off). The admin page at 192.168.8.1 must open over the cable too.
  7. B7. Global or CN version. In the admin page's left menu, look for a VPN section (OpenVPN, WireGuard). Present = Global: can be MAIN. Missing = CN version (GL.iNet removes VPN from it): keep it only as SPARE, and return it if a Global unit is easy to get within the window. We replace the factory software with official OpenWrt anyway, so GL's missing VPN menu does not matter to us; forum users report OpenWrt works on CN units, but GL.iNet does not confirm it and Wi-Fi limits there are unknown. A CN unit becomes MAIN only after we flash it and Wi-Fi works on 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz channels 36–48.

Why B5 is decisive. A different board cannot report glinet,gl-mt3000 together with a MediaTek MT7981 and 512 MB. Later, the official OpenWrt image is built for exactly this board and refuses to install on anything else: that is the final proof, done only on the unit you keep as MAIN.

Expected values for B5 come from how GL.iNet firmware (OpenWrt-based) reports this board; the exact free-memory figure varies by a few MB with the firmware version. If a value differs, photograph the screen and ask before returning.

C. Keep or return

Decision per unit
ResultAction
all of A and B passKeep. Put a sticker on it: MAIN (first Global one) or SPARE. Keep the box, all packaging and the receipt until the return window has closed.
only a missing accessoryUsually keep (any 5 V / 3 A USB-C charger works). Note it in the record.
any of B1–B6 failsReturn within the window, with photos of the failing screen and of the label. Reset to factory first (hold reset about 10 s) so your admin password is not on it.
CN version (A8 / B7)SPARE only. If you already have a Global MAIN and SPARE, return it. If no Global unit passed, keep it and tell me: we test-flash OpenWrt on it before relying on it.
A third unit that passesReturn it within the window, or keep it as a second spare if the cost is acceptable.

Distance purchases in Russia can normally be returned within 7 days even without a defect; orders shipped by foreign (cross-border) sellers may follow different, slower rules. Check the return terms on each order page before ordering. Not verified for each marketplace.

Record sheet

Fill one column per unit. Keep a photo of this sheet with the router kit; it tells you later which unit is which.

Typical mistakes

Accepting before looking

Once you confirm the pickup code and leave, refusing turns into a return. Look at the box and the label at the counter.

No photos

Without photos of the sealed box and the label, a dispute about "used" or "wrong model" is your word against the seller's.

Throwing the box away

Returns usually need the full packaging. Keep everything until the return window closes.

Flashing too early

Installing OpenWrt before the checks, or on the spare, can make a return harder. Flash only the MAIN unit, after it passed, and only when we start the router setup.

Weak charger

A 5 V / 1–2 A phone charger makes the router reboot under load. It looks like a faulty unit but is not. Use 5 V / 3 A (15 W) or more.

Wrong port

The WAN port (2.5G) is for the incoming internet; the laptop goes into LAN. Nothing needs the WAN port during this check.

Returning over a MAC "mismatch"

The Wi-Fi, LAN and WAN interfaces can show MACs that differ from the label in the last one or two characters. That is normal; a completely different MAC is not.

Cloud account and weak password

Do not bind the router to GoodCloud and do not keep a short admin password. We set our own configuration later; cloud management stays off.

Mixing up units

Check one unit at a time and stick MAIN / SPARE on it immediately. Two identical boxes are easy to swap.

Returning with your password on it

Before sending a unit back, hold the reset button about 10 seconds so it returns to factory state.

Router setup: GL-MT3000 with OpenWrt and Podkop

A complete manual path from a new GL-MT3000 (Global or CN) to a router whose Wi-Fi sends everything through our VLESS + Reality server. It works without the chat session: every command is here, and each step says where it runs. Global and CN units follow the same path: we replace GL.iNet's software with official OpenWrt, so the CN restrictions disappear with it.

~60 min
first unit, with internet available
25.12.6
official OpenWrt, sysupgrade image (checksum below)
0.7.24
Podkop release (2026-10-11), sing-box 1.13 from OpenWrt

Before step 1: the unit has passed the arrival check (A1–A8 and B1–B7). Flash only a unit you are keeping. Secrets (VLESS links, Wi-Fi and admin passwords) come from the password manager and never go into files or chat.

Where a step runs: Mac = a terminal on your laptop (prefer your personal laptop: the work Mac is managed and its network settings or GlobalProtect may interfere); browser = the laptop's browser; router = after ssh root@…. Addresses: stock GL firmware 192.168.8.1, recovery mode and fresh OpenWrt 192.168.1.1.

Global or CN: what differs for this guide

Same path, three differences
StepGlobal unitCN unit
1. Install OpenWrtStock web page, Local Upgrade (path A).Try path A. If the stock page refuses the file or has no Local Upgrade, use recovery mode (path B).
4. Wi-FiSet the country, check channels.Same, and check carefully that 5 GHz channels 36–48 and 2.4 GHz work (step 4, check W3). If not: keep as spare, do not use as MAIN.
RoleMAIN or SPARE.SPARE unless it passes step 4 and step 6.

We do not "patch" a CN unit to Global. The known patch writes a country code into the router's Factory partition with dd. That partition also holds the Wi-Fi calibration data: one wrong byte can leave the unit without working Wi-Fi or unbootable. It is unofficial (GL.iNet: "No, this isn't supported") and only matters if you want GL.iNet's own software, which we do not use. Official OpenWrt ignores GL's region setting and uses its own country setting (forum users report CN units work "the same as others"; not confirmed by GL.iNet or OpenWrt).

0. Kit and downloads (Mac, while internet works)

Needed: the router, a USB-C charger of 5 V / 3 A or more, the Ethernet cable from the box, a laptop with an Ethernet port or USB-C Ethernet adapter, internet for the router (a cable from another router, or a Wi-Fi network you know the password of), the VLESS links from the password manager.

The image is also cached in the project at .private/downloads/router-kit/ (checked 2026-11-09). To download it again, on the Mac:

mkdir -p ~/router-kit && cd ~/router-kit
curl -fLO https://downloads.openwrt.org/releases/25.12.6/targets/mediatek/filogic/openwrt-25.12.6-mediatek-filogic-glinet_gl-mt3000-squashfs-sysupgrade.bin
shasum -a 256 openwrt-25.12.6-mediatek-filogic-glinet_gl-mt3000-squashfs-sysupgrade.bin

The printed checksum must be exactly:

c2965b9d49d2ff42bf00c4f04ef73eaae904f553c68af47332fec702b30bf6f4

If it differs, delete the file and download again; never flash a file with a different checksum. There is no separate "factory" image for this model: the sysupgrade image is used for both paths. A newer 25.12.x may exist later: then take its sysupgrade file and its line from the sha256sums file in the same folder.

1. Install OpenWrt

Path A: from the stock GL.iNet page (try first)

  1. Cable. Router powered, laptop plugged into the LAN port (not WAN), laptop Wi-Fi off. On the work Mac, disconnect GlobalProtect from its menu first.
  2. Browser: open http://192.168.8.1 and log in with the admin password set during the arrival check.
  3. Left menu SYSTEM → Upgrade, tab Local Upgrade. Choose the …squashfs-sysupgrade.bin file.
  4. Untick "Keep Settings". GL.iNet settings must not be carried into OpenWrt.
  5. Confirm the install. Do not unplug power for 5 minutes. The LED blinks, then settles.
  6. The router now lives at 192.168.1.1. Unplug and replug the cable so the laptop picks up a new address, then go to step 2.

GL.iNet's documentation describes Local Upgrade for its own firmware files; whether the stock page accepts an official OpenWrt file is not documented (widely done by users; on a CN unit unknown). If it refuses the file, use path B; nothing has changed on the router.

1b. Path B: recovery mode (U-Boot web page)

Use it when path A refuses the file, after a failed flash, or to go back to GL.iNet firmware. It cannot be broken by a bad image: you can always repeat it. Source: GL.iNet "debrick" documentation (dated 2026-10-22).

  1. Power off the router. Laptop cable into the LAN port; nothing in WAN.
  2. Laptop address (Mac): System Settings → Network → the Ethernet adapter → Details → TCP/IP → Configure IPv4: Manually. IP address 192.168.1.2, Subnet mask 255.255.255.0, Router 192.168.1.1. Turn off any VPN or proxy on the laptop (GlobalProtect disconnected).
  3. Hold the reset button firmly with a pin, and while holding it, plug in power. The blue LED flashes 6 times, then turns solid white: release the button. GL.iNet notes that other production batches can show different colours or blink patterns; release when the pattern changes.
  4. Browser: http://192.168.1.1 shows a plain upgrade page. Choose file → the …squashfs-sysupgrade.bin → Update firmware.
  5. Wait about 3 minutes; do not unplug power.
  6. Set the Mac back to Using DHCP (same settings page), replug the cable, go to step 2.

GL.iNet documents this page for its own firmware; that it also accepts the official OpenWrt sysupgrade image is reported by users, not documented (UNVERIFIED). If it is refused, stop and ask (see "When stuck").

2. First login and password

Mac (the cable still in LAN; a fresh OpenWrt has no password yet, so the login asks none). If ssh warns that the host key changed, run the first line, then the second:

ssh-keygen -R 192.168.1.1
ssh root@192.168.1.1

On the router: check what runs, then set the admin password (store it in the password manager first):

cat /etc/openwrt_release
ubus call system board
passwd

Expected: DISTRIB_RELEASE='25.12.6', "board_name": "glinet,gl-mt3000". Then the browser: http://192.168.1.1 opens the OpenWrt web page (LuCI); log in as root with the new password.

If the web page does not open: official release images normally include it. Install it after step 3 gives the router internet: on the router apk update, then apk add luci.

Browser: System → System → General: Timezone Europe/Moscow (or your current one) → Save & Apply.

3. Internet into the router

Option 1: cable (simplest, use it for setup)

A cable from the apartment's router into the WAN port (2.5G). OpenWrt asks for an address automatically. Check on the router:

ping -c 3 1.1.1.1

Option 2: someone else's Wi-Fi (hotel, apartment without cable)

  1. Browser: Network → Wireless. On the radio of the band you want (2.4 GHz reaches further) click Scan.
  2. Next to the network click Join Network. Do not tick "Replace wireless configuration". Name: wwan. Enter its password. Firewall zone: wan. Submit, then Save & Apply.
  3. Check with ping -c 3 1.1.1.1 on the router.

The router's own Wi-Fi then runs on the same channel as that network (one radio does both). A login page (captive portal) in a hotel must be completed from a laptop connected to the router, before Podkop is on, or with the laptop on the hotel Wi-Fi directly. Automatic switching between known networks (travelmate) comes with the setup script later; not needed for the first test.

4. Wi-Fi from the router

Fresh OpenWrt usually starts with Wi-Fi switched off. Browser: Network → Wireless. For each radio (2.4 GHz and 5 GHz) click Edit:

  1. Device Configuration → Advanced Settings → Country Code: the country you are in now (GE Georgia, RU Russia).
  2. Operating frequency: 5 GHz: mode AX, channel 36, width 80 MHz. 2.4 GHz: mode AX, channel 1, 6 or 11, width 20 MHz.
  3. Interface Configuration → General: ESSID WORK (same name on both radios), Network lan. Wireless Security: WPA2-PSK/WPA3-SAE Mixed Mode, a strong key from the password manager.
  4. Save, then Enable the radio, then Save & Apply.

Checks on the router:

iw reg get
iwinfo
Wi-Fi checks (the ones that matter for a CN unit)
#CheckPass
W1iw reg getThe country line shows the code you set (GE or RU), not CN.
W2iwinfoTwo access-point interfaces named WORK, one on channel 36, one on 1, 6 or 11, each with a non-zero Tx-Power.
W3Phone and laptopBoth see WORK, connect, and a phone 2 rooms away still holds the 5 GHz network.

A CN unit that fails W1–W3 after setting the country stays SPARE; note the output and ask. Later the setup script adds the second network DIRECT (no tunnel) and moves the router to its own address range.

5. Podkop: send everything through the server

Requires internet in the router (step 3). On the router, set the clock (certificate checks fail without it), then install Podkop with its official script:

ntpd -q -p 0.openwrt.pool.ntp.org
sh <(wget -O - https://raw.githubusercontent.com/itdoginfo/podkop/refs/heads/main/install.sh)

The script asks in Russian whether to install the Russian translation: n for English, y for Russian. It installs podkop, luci-app-podkop and sing-box (1.13.x from OpenWrt; Podkop needs 1.12.4 or newer).

If GitHub is unreachable from the router, copy the two Podkop files from .private/downloads/router-kit/ (Podkop 0.7.24) to the router with scp -O podkop-0.7.24-r1.apk luci-app-podkop-0.7.24-r1.apk root@192.168.1.1:/tmp/ on the Mac, then on the router apk update and apk add --allow-untrusted /tmp/podkop-0.7.24-r1.apk /tmp/luci-app-podkop-0.7.24-r1.apk. apk update still needs the OpenWrt package server (for sing-box).

Browser: reload, then Services → Podkop. In the main section:

Podkop settings for "everything from WORK through the server"
SettingValueWhy
Connection typeProxyVLESS is a proxy link, not a VPN interface.
Configuration TypeConnection URL while only server A exists; URLTest once server B existsURLTest picks the working link automatically (failover).
Link(s)The Vision link of server A (port 443) from the password manager; with URLTest also server B's Vision linkOnly Vision links; the XHTTP link (port 8443) is a test variant and needs a special sing-box build.
Fully Routed IPs192.168.1.0/24 (the router's LAN range)Sends all traffic of every device on WORK through the tunnel, not only listed sites.
Source Network Interfacebr-lan (default)The bridge that WORK belongs to.
DNSleave the defaultsChecked in step 6; tuned later by the setup script.
Community lists, domain listsnoneNot needed when everything is routed.

Save & Apply. Then on the router:

/usr/bin/podkop show_version
/usr/bin/podkop global_check

Option names are from Podkop's documentation (podkop.net, 2026-11). Untested here: that a Vision link pastes as-is, and that URLTest with several links works on the standard sing-box (the README mentions an alternative build for "fallback links"). If the link is refused, ask; the fallback is the "Outbound Config" type with a sing-box JSON outbound.

6. Verify

Pass all before relying on the router
✓#WhereCheckPass
V1BrowserServices → Podkop → Diagnostics → Run diagnosticsNo red items. A failing "FakeIP" item is expected when everything is routed (Fully Routed IPs).
V2Phone on WORK, mobile data offOpen an "what is my IP" page (e.g. ifconfig.me)Shows server A's address (compare with the password manager entry), not the local provider.
V3Phone on WORKA 2–3 minute video, a speed testPlays smoothly; speed roughly like the Russian-PC test (7–11 Mbit/s or better).
V4Routerreboot, wait 2 minutes, repeat V2Works again without touching anything.
V5RouterUnplug WAN for 1 minute, plug back, repeat V2 after 1 minuteRecovers by itself.
V6PhoneLeave connected overnightStill works in the morning.

In Georgia these checks prove the router setup, not that it passes Russian filtering; that part is proven by the Russian-PC tests and on day 1 in Russia.

7. Backup and the spare unit

  1. Browser: System → Backup / Flash Firmware → Generate archive. The file contains the VLESS link and Wi-Fi passwords: store it in the password manager as an attachment, not in the project or a chat.
  2. Spare unit: steps 1 and 2 on the spare, then System → Backup / Flash Firmware → Restore backup with that archive. Then install Podkop (step 5, install part only; settings come from the backup) and run step 6. Same model, so the backup restores 1:1. Do this only after the spare's return window has closed, or once you are sure to keep it.

8. Back to GL.iNet stock firmware (if ever needed)

For a return to the seller or to start over. In a browser on the Mac open https://dl.gl-inet.com/router/mt3000/, download the current stable firmware in its U-Boot variant (GL: "Please download the U-Boot compatible firmware"), then follow 1b with that file. Afterwards the stock page is back at 192.168.8.1. A CN unit returns to its CN firmware's behaviour only if you flash CN firmware; for a return to the seller this does not matter for the unit's function.

When stuck

Page does not open

Check the cable is in LAN, Wi-Fi is off, GlobalProtect is disconnected, and the Mac is on DHCP (except during 1b). Replug the cable.

Flash failed, LED odd

Nothing is lost: do 1b. Recovery mode normally lives in a separate part of the flash that an upgrade does not touch.

No internet after Podkop

Services → Podkop → Stop; if internet returns, the link or server is the problem (check V2 from the phone app with the same link).

Need help in a new session

Open the project in Claude Code and say "router setup, step N, here is the output". Paste output, never links or passwords.

Russia connectivity: gated rollout plan

Every phase answers one question. Money and time go into the next phase only after the current gate passes.

Prepared 5 November 2026 for the implementing agent. Censorship in Russia changes week to week; re-check Appendix D before starting Phase 2.

How to use this plan

  • Run phases in order. Do not start a phase until the gate before it has passed, except where Parallel work says otherwise.
  • For every gate, keep the evidence listed in the Gate summary in a run log (a plain document with dates, logs and screenshots).
  • Thresholds are defaults. Change one only with a written reason in the run log.
  • Keys, passwords, subscription links and configs never go into this document, chat logs or the run log. They live in a password manager (see Appendix E).
  • The user is a confident computer user but not a network specialist. Give step-by-step instructions, ask yes/no questions, and make the technical decisions yourself.

Ordering rule

The cheapest question that can kill the plan goes first. Each row lists what a negative answer saves.

PhaseQuestionCost to find outA “no” saves you
0Can we run meaningful tests from inside Russia?$0Designing tests nobody can run
1Can Russian ISPs reach the hosting providers we would rent from?$0Renting servers that are already blocked
2Do our tunnel protocols survive Russian filtering, reliably and fast enough?≈ $15–25Buying routers, a domain and annual plans
3Do they also work on real home and mobile ISPs?$0False confidence from one office line
4Does the work laptop need a router in front of it?$0Buying hardware that adds nothing
5Does the full router stack work end to end?One returnable routerBuying the second router
6–9Commit, prepare, arrive, operateSecond router, annual plansNothing; premises are verified

Click a box to jump to its section. Dashed boxes are loops or side branches; red boxes stop the self-hosted track.

What we are building

  • Two servers at different non-Russian providers, in different countries and networks. Each runs 3x-ui (Xray) with VLESS + Reality using its own domain for camouflage (“self-steal”) and VLESS + XHTTP, plus AmneziaWG 3.1 installed by the Amnezia app.
  • Two identical routers (GL.iNet Beryl AX preferred) on official OpenWrt with Podkop. Podkop’s URLTest switches automatically between both servers’ VLESS + Reality links. Travelmate handles hotel Wi-Fi. Two Wi-Fi networks: WORK (everything through the tunnel) and DIRECT (no tunnel).
  • Phones and the personal laptop use apps directly: a subscription client (Hiddify, Happ or v2RayTun) with both servers, and the Amnezia app with AmneziaWG 3.1 keys.
  • Commercial backup: Amnezia Premium, bought close to departure.
  • Monitoring: a scheduled probe on RU-PC until arrival.

Work laptop with GlobalProtect or AWS VPN → router WORK Wi-Fi → VLESS + Reality → server A or B → corporate gateway

0

Feasibility and baseline

Can we run meaningful tests from inside Russia, and what does the network block today?

Owner
User and agent
Cost
$0
Time
One evening
Starts after
Nothing

Every later gate relies on evidence from RU-PC. If it cannot install tools, drops the remote session, or sits behind a proxy that hides real filtering, the test design changes before any money is spent.

  1. 0.1
    Employer authorization. User Confirm with the employer that working from Russia and connecting GlobalProtect and AWS Client VPN from there is permitted, and that RU-PC may be used for network tests and test software. Do not design the setup to disguise the work location from the employer. If remote work from Russia is not permitted, the work-laptop track (Phases 4–5) loses its purpose; the personal track continues.
  2. 0.2
    RU-PC audit. Agent
    • Operating system and version, admin rights, ability to install software (curl, a proxy client, Python if needed).
    • Remote desktop stability over at least two hours; whether the machine can stay on overnight.
    • Public IP, its ISP name and ASN (for example from ipinfo.io). It must be a Russian ISP, not a data center or a foreign proxy.
    • Whether outbound UDP and TCP on ports other than 443 work.
    • Whether a corporate proxy intercepts TLS: inspect the certificate issuer of a known HTTPS site.
  3. 0.3
    Service inventory. User and agent Build services.txt with one URL per line, tagged by group:
    • A: blocked in Russia, must go through the tunnel.
    • B: Russian services (banks, Gosuslugi, Yandex, marketplaces), must go direct.
    • C: foreign services that refuse Russian IPs (AI services, some banks and streaming), tunnel only, no leaks.
    • D: work endpoints: the GlobalProtect portal hostname and the AWS Client VPN endpoint hostname, protocol and port from the .ovpn file.
  4. 0.4
    Direct baseline from RU-PC, no tunnel. Agent Run test T4 (Appendix A) without the proxy flag. Record which group A sites fail (expected) and which group B sites work. For group D: DNS resolves, TCP 443 connects, and the GlobalProtect prelogin page loads (Appendix A, D-checks).
  5. 0.5
    Open the run log and store the audit notes and baseline output. Agent

Gate G0: is RU-PC a usable and representative probe?

Pass when

  • Test tools install and run.
  • The remote session stays up for two hours or more.
  • Traffic leaves through a Russian ISP, not a data center or foreign proxy.
  • At least some group A sites fail directly, which proves filtering is applied on this line.

If it fails

  • Switch to Branch F3: friends’ phones become the primary probes, with Phase 3 procedures used earlier and more often.
  • If a corporate proxy blocks all non-web traffic, results will be too pessimistic: never reject a protocol on RU-PC evidence alone.

Unlocks Phase 1.

1

Hosting reachability

Which hosting providers can a Russian ISP reach at all?

Owner
Agent
Cost
$0, no purchases
Time
One evening
Starts after
G0 (or F3)

Whole provider networks get throttled or blocked. Checking subnets first costs nothing and keeps us from renting servers that are dead on arrival.

  1. 1.1
    Shortlist four to six providers. Requirements: non-Russian company; KVM virtualization; dedicated IPv4; Ubuntu 22.04 or Debian 11+ images; hourly billing or a refund window; accepts a foreign card; at least three distinct countries and networks across the list. Include Amnezia Hosting (Netherlands) as one candidate.

    Exclude: AWS, Oracle Cloud, DigitalOcean, OVH, Hetzner, Scaleway, Akamai/Linode (known throttling from Russia); Russian-owned hosters including their foreign locations (2026 hosting rules); FirstVDS (October 2026 breach).

  2. 1.2
    Collect sample IPs and subnets for each candidate: looking-glass pages, provider documentation, or a short-lived hourly test server.
  3. 1.3
    Run TSPU_checker from RU-PC against each candidate subnet, and test T1 against sample IPs on ports 22 and 443.
  4. 1.4
    Rank the candidates and record the results in the run log.

Gate G1: are two or more providers reachable?

Pass when

  • At least two providers in different networks (ideally different countries) show no subnet-level blocking from RU-PC.

If it fails

  • Extend the shortlist and repeat 1.1–1.3.
  • After ten candidates without two passes, stop and ask the user whether to switch to Branch F1.

Unlocks Phase 2.

2

Protocol validation from Russia

Do our tunnel protocols survive Russian filtering, reliably and fast enough?

Owner
Agent
Cost
≈ $15–25: two short-term servers and a domain
Time
2–3 evenings plus a 24-hour soak
Starts after
G1

This is the main go/no-go. If no protocol passes, routers, annual plans and the domain are all wasted. Rent the shortest billing period available.

Never enable a full-tunnel VPN on RU-PC. It will cut the remote desktop session. Use local proxy mode, split tunnelling, route-nopull for OpenVPN, or limited AllowedIPs for AmneziaWG.

  1. 2.1
    Rent server A and server B at the two best providers from G1. Harden both: SSH keys only, password login off, firewall allowing only SSH, 443/tcp and the AmneziaWG UDP port, automatic security updates.
  2. 2.2
    Deploy the stack on each server.
    • 3x-ui (Xray). Inbound 1: VLESS + Reality on 443/tcp; for now use a neutral, non-brand camouflage site, never Google, Microsoft, Apple or other big brands. Inbound 2: VLESS + XHTTP.
    • Panel reachable only through an SSH tunnel, never exposed publicly.
    • AmneziaWG 3.1 installed from GE-PC with the Amnezia app. Do not install the app’s own Xray container: it would conflict with 3x-ui on port 443.
  3. 2.3
    OpenVPN probe (feeds G4). Run a temporary OpenVPN server on server B (UDP 1194 and TCP on a spare port). Connect from RU-PC with route-nopull and keep it up for ten minutes. AWS Client VPN uses OpenVPN, so if this is blocked, AWS Client VPN will be too. Remove the OpenVPN server afterwards.
  4. 2.4
    Reference check from GE-PC: each profile connects, the visible IP is the server’s, DNS leak test is clean, throughput is recorded.
  5. 2.5
    Tests from RU-PC for every server and profile: T1 port reachability, T2 three-minute series, T3 50 MB download, T4 service list through the tunnel, T5 24-hour soak (Appendix A). AmneziaWG goes through split tunnelling only.
  6. 2.6
    Domain and self-steal. Buy a non-.ru domain at an international registrar with privacy protection. Point it at server A (and a subdomain at B). Run a small web server with a valid certificate on each server and switch Reality to camouflage as that site. Re-run T1–T4.
  7. 2.7
    Fill the pass matrix: server × profile × test, with links to logs.

Gate G2: do the protocols survive from Russia?

Pass when, on both servers

  • At least one VLESS profile passes T2 with 9 of 9 requests.
  • T3 completes without a stall longer than 10 seconds.
  • T4 reaches every group A and C service.
  • T5 succeeds in 97% or more of checks over 24 hours.
  • Median throughput is at least 20 Mbit/s, or half of RU-PC’s direct speed, whichever is lower.
  • AmneziaWG 3.1 results are recorded; they matter for phones, not for routers.

If it fails

  • Iterate, up to three rounds: new IP from another /24, different camouflage site or browser fingerprint, switch to XHTTP, swap in the next provider from G1.
  • Still failing: Branch F1. Do not buy routers before G2 passes.

Unlocks Phases 3 and 4, which can run in parallel.

G2

Filtering differs by ISP and region. The office line is one data point; the user will live on a home ISP and sometimes on mobile.

  1. 3.1
    Create one client per friend in 3x-ui with a 14-day expiry and a traffic cap (for example 10 GB). Never share the user’s own keys.
  2. 3.2
    Send the instructions from Appendix B, translated to Russian.

    Collect results into an ISP × server × profile matrix. Note whether mobile tests ran during whitelist mode.

Gate G3: does it pass on two or more home ISPs?

Pass when

  • At least one server works on two or more different home ISPs, preferably including the ISP at the user’s future address.
  • Mobile results are informational: whitelist mode cannot be fixed by any setup.

If it fails

  • Office passes but homes fail means ISP-specific blocking. Return to Phase 2 iteration using the failing friend as the reference probe.

Work-path decision

Does the work laptop need a router in front of it?

Owner
Agent, user decides
Cost
$0
Time
One hour
Starts after
G2 and 0.1

The router exists only to carry the corporate VPNs inside the tunnel. If they work directly and reliably from Russia, the router is optional.

  1. 4.1
    Gather evidence: group D results from 0.4, the OpenVPN probe from 2.3, and, if the employer allows it, a real GlobalProtect and AWS Client VPN session on RU-PC.
  2. 4.2
    Apply the decision rule. A router is required if any of these is true: the OpenVPN probe is blocked or unstable; the GlobalProtect portal or gateway is unreachable or unstable directly; the corporate VPN clients cannot coexist with the personal tunnel on the laptop. A router is optional only if both corporate VPNs connect directly from RU-PC and stay stable through a full work session.

Gate G4: does the work laptop need a router?

Yes

  • Go to Phase 5.

No

  • Branch F2: no router, apps on devices, continue at Phase 6. The user may still choose a router for resilience.
5

Router pilot, one unit

Does the full router stack work end to end, and does its exact configuration pass in Russia?

Owner
User (hands), agent
Cost
One router, ≈ $70–90, returnable
Time
1–2 evenings plus 3 days
Starts after
G2, G3, G4 = yes

The router cannot be tested inside Russia, but it does not need to be: Russia-dependent behaviour is already validated in Phases 2–3. Here we validate everything router-dependent in Georgia, then run the router’s exact configuration on RU-PC.

  1. 5.1
    Buy one unit of the best available model (Appendix C). Confirm the return window and whether a unit is accepted after stock firmware is restored. Alternative: buy two and keep the second sealed. Record model, hardware revision and serial number.
  2. 5.2
    Day zero on stock firmware: powers on, Wi-Fi visible, admin page opens, stock firmware updates. Any defect: return immediately.
  3. 5.3
    Flash official OpenWrt. Choose the stable release that Podkop and the needed packages support on that day. Have the recovery procedure ready before flashing (U-Boot web recovery on GL.iNet, vendor intermediate firmware on Cudy).
  4. 5.4
    Configure.
    • Podkop with URLTest across the VLESS + Reality links of servers A and B (a subscription script is optional).
    • DNS resolved through the tunnel.
    • WORK Wi-Fi: everything through the tunnel. DIRECT Wi-Fi: no tunnel.
    • Travelmate for hotel Wi-Fi and captive portals.
    • MSS clamping on; WAN tested with MTU 1492 to imitate Russian PPPoE lines.
    • Strong admin password; remote and cloud management off.
  5. 5.5
    Tests in Georgia, T6–T10 (Appendix A): function, failover, a full work session with both corporate VPNs, every WAN mode, three-day burn-in.
  6. 5.6
    Router twin on RU-PC. Export the sing-box configuration Podkop generates, replace the router-specific inbounds with a local proxy inbound, and run T2–T5 on RU-PC. The closest alternative is an OpenWrt x86 virtual machine on RU-PC with the same Podkop settings.
  7. 5.7
    Back up the router configuration and store it in the password manager.

Gate G5: do the stack and twin tests pass?

Pass when

  • T6–T10 pass in Georgia.
  • The twin configuration passes T2–T5 on RU-PC.

If it fails

  • Fix configuration issues (MTU, DNS, routing) and re-test.
  • Hardware or model problem: restore stock firmware, repack, return; take the next model from Appendix C and repeat 5.1.

Unlocks Phase 6.

G5Do the stack and twin tests pass?T6–T10 log, twin T2–T5 log, router backupFix, or restore stock firmware and return

Fallback branches

F1. Commercial only

Taken when G1 or G2 fails after the allowed iterations. Use Amnezia Premium plus a second commercial service from a different company on phones and laptops. No routers. Corporate VPN access from Russia may then be impossible; escalate to the user and, through them, the employer.

F2. No router

Taken when G4 says the corporate VPNs work directly. Keep the two servers and apps on every device. The corporate VPN runs alone on the work laptop. One router remains an optional purchase for resilience.

F3. Degraded probing

Taken when G0 fails. Friends’ phones become the main probes for Phases 1–2. Expect slower cycles and fewer controlled measurements; require results from at least two friends on different ISPs before passing G2.

Parallel work

  • Employer authorization (0.1) can start immediately and run alongside everything else.
  • Phases 3 and 4 run in parallel after G2.
  • If the router takes more than seven days to arrive, it may be ordered after G2 instead of after G3, accepting a small return risk. Never order before G2.
  • The domain is bought only in step 2.6, after the first protocol results.

Appendix A. Test procedures

All tunnel tests use a client that exposes a local SOCKS5 or mixed proxy at 127.0.0.1:1080. On Linux use xray-core or the sing-box CLI. On Windows use the sing-box CLI, v2rayN or Hiddify and substitute their local port. Windows 10 and later include curl.exe; run the bash examples in WSL or Git Bash, or adapt them to PowerShell.

T1. Port reachability

nc -zv -w5 SERVER_IP 443
# Windows PowerShell:
Test-NetConnection SERVER_IP -Port 443

T2. Three-minute series

Some blocks trigger only after the first kilobytes or after a delay, so a single request proves nothing. Pass: 9 of 9 responses with a 2xx or 3xx code.

for i in $(seq 1 9); do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -m 20 --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 \
    -w "$(date +%T) %{http_code} %{time_total}s\n" https://www.instagram.com
  sleep 20
done

T3. Large download

Catches freezes after about 16 KB and measures throughput. Pass: completes, no stall over 10 seconds.

curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 -o /dev/null -m 120 \
  -w "%{size_download} bytes, %{speed_download} B/s\n" \
  "https://speed.cloudflare.com/__down?bytes=50000000"

T4. Service list

Run once through the tunnel and once without --socks5-hostname for the direct baseline.

while read url; do
  printf "%-45s " "$url"
  curl -s -o /dev/null -m 15 --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 -w "%{http_code}\n" "$url"
done < services.txt

T5. Soak

Run one client instance per server and profile on its own local port (1081, 1082 and so on). Schedule the probe every 5 minutes with cron or Windows Task Scheduler. Pass: 97% or more rows return 204 in under 5 seconds over 24 hours.

# probe.sh LABEL PORT
ts=$(date -u +%FT%TZ)
r=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -m 20 --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:$2 \
     -w "%{http_code},%{time_total}" https://www.gstatic.com/generate_204)
echo "$ts,$1,$r" >> soak.csv

D-checks. Corporate endpoints

TLS reachability only; no credentials are used. Run direct and through the tunnel.

curl -sv -m 15 -o /dev/null https://GP_PORTAL/global-protect/prelogin.esp

For AWS Client VPN, rely on the OpenVPN probe from step 2.3; a reachable port does not show whether the OpenVPN handshake itself is blocked.

T6–T10. Router tests in Georgia

TestWhat to doPass when
T6On WORK Wi-Fi: visible IP, DNS leak test, T4 service listServer IP, no leaks, all group A and C reachable
T7Stop Xray on server A; watch traffic; start it againTraffic moves to B within a minute and back without manual action
T8Work laptop on WORK Wi-Fi: GlobalProtect, then AWS Client VPN; 30+ minute video call, large download, git and sshBoth connect and stay stable; no stalls on large transfers
T9WAN modes: Ethernet, Wi-Fi repeater, USB tethering from a phone; reboot in each modeTunnel comes back on its own in every mode

Appendix B. Friend instructions

Translate into Russian before sending. Send the link or QR code in a separate message.

  1. Install Hiddify. If it is not in your app store, install Happ or v2RayTun instead.
  2. Open the link or QR code I sent and import it into the app. Connect.
  3. Open these sites: [5–6 sites from groups A and C]. Play a YouTube video for two minutes.
  4. Run a speed test on fast.com.
  5. Leave a video playing for 30 minutes and note whether it stops.
  6. Repeat everything on mobile data, and once more in the evening between 19:00 and 23:00.
  7. Send me: city, home ISP, mobile operator, times of the tests, what did not work, screenshots of errors, and whether most foreign sites were dead on mobile even without the app (that means whitelist mode).

The key expires in 14 days.

Buy two of the same model. Ranked by preference:

1GL.iNet Beryl AX (GL-MT3000)Pocket size, USB-C power, MediaTek MT7981B, 512 MB RAM, mature official OpenWrt support, stock firmware as a fallbackExactly GL-MT3000; not GL-MT1300 (old Beryl) or GL-MT3600BE (Beryl 7). USB-C 5V/3A adapter included

Appendix D. Known constraints, November 2026

  • Plain WireGuard and OpenVPN are blocked in Russia since February 2026.
  • Filtering judges traffic behaviour after roughly the first 16 KB, checks whether the camouflage site matches the hosting, and since August 2026 blocks whole subnets of hosters popular with VPNs. Rollout differs by ISP and region.
  • Large clouds (AWS, DigitalOcean, OVH, Oracle Cloud, Scaleway, Akamai, Hetzner) are often throttled from Russia.
  • Data-center networks inside Russia are filtered less than home ISPs, which is why RU-PC on an office ISP is a better probe than a Russian VPS.
  • Mobile internet in many regions periodically switches to whitelist mode; only allowlisted IPs are reachable and no tunnel helps.
  • AmneziaWG 1.5 and 2.0 have become vulnerable to blocking; Amnezia recommends 3.1 for self-hosted servers. Versions 2.0 and 3.1 share one container and cannot run side by side from the app.
  • Router firmware (Keenetic, OpenWrt, GL.iNet) does not support AmneziaWG 3.x yet, so routers use VLESS.
  • Podkop is in beta, needs OpenWrt 24.10 or later, and its URLTest mode does not accept XHTTP links.
  • Since 2026, Russian hosting providers may not host VPN infrastructure. FirstVDS suffered a breach on 17 October 2026 that exposed root passwords and SSH keys.
  • Many popular Russian apps detect an active VPN, so split tunnelling for Russian services is required.

Appendix E. Security rules

  • Secrets live only in the password manager, with an encrypted offline copy. Never in this document, the run log, chats or email.
  • Servers: SSH keys only, password login off, firewall with the minimum open ports, automatic security updates, panels reachable only through an SSH tunnel.
  • Every person and device gets its own client key, so one can be revoked without touching the others. Friends’ keys expire.
  • Routers: strong admin password, remote and cloud management off, configuration backed up after every change.
  • A lost or stolen router means revoking its keys on both servers the same day.
  • RU-PC: install only what the tests need and remove test tools after Phase 7 unless monitoring still runs; follow the employer’s rules for that machine.
